terminal_bridge: lost during a crash. However, recording that an action occurred does not solve the problem of what to do when an external action *fails midway* through a complex multi-step mutation. In distributed systems involving heterogeneous third-party services, cloud platforms, and developer tooling, atomic multi-system updates cannot rely on distributed transactions or two-phase commit ($2\text{PC}$) protocols; external APIs rarely expose prepare phases, and holding distributed locks across non-deterministic LLM deliberation intervals violates basic availability invariants. When a long-horizon trajectory encounters partial failure—such as provisioning a cloud compute instance and modifying DNS records, but failing on firewall configuration—the durable event log provides the exact historical trail of executed operations, but cannot alone unwind or heal the inconsistent remote environment. In Chapter 11 (*Fault Recovery*), we shift from passive durability to active operational remediation. We examine how the Agent Runtime coordinates distributed failure recovery through Hector Garcia-Molina's Saga pattern, executing compensating transactions ($\tau^{-1}$) in reverse causal order to unwind side effects when forward progress stalls. We analyze forward recovery through model-mediated self-healing, where the supervisor feeds diagnostic compiler traces and execution exceptions back to the unprivileged model to synthesize corrective patches. Finally, we explore semantic watchdogs and hardware-enforced supervisor timeouts that detect and break infinite execution loops, ensuring that agentic systems maintain structural invariants even when operating in an unreliable, adversarial world. :::
cumulative_ledger: Section 10.1 (Append-Only Event Sourcing): An append-only event history preserves what the runtime knew, authorized, and observed, while current-state projections make operational resumption efficient; mutable in-place updates destroy causal auditability.

Section 10.2 (Write-Ahead Logging Discipline): Runtimes must strictly enforce Write-Ahead Logging (WAL): never dispatch a mutating tool action before the corresponding event record is durably flushed to non-volatile storage via `fsync()`.

Section 10.3 (Periodic State Checkpointing): Periodic state snapshots bound recovery time; runtimes must optimize checkpoint intervals by balancing snapshot write latency against expected replay recomputation cost.

Section 10.4 (Historical Trajectory Reconstruction): Trajectory reconstruction uses recorded model responses, authorization decisions, and observations to rebuild the known control state without repeating external side effects; re-running a stochastic model is a new computation, not bit-exact replay.

Section 10.5 (Replay Divergence Diagnostics): Bit-exact trajectory replay is disrupted by non-deterministic sampling, floating-point kernel race conditions, and dynamic wall-clocks; runtimes must virtualize and record all entropy sources.

Section 10.6 (Live Trajectory Migration): Decoupling execution state into serialized ACBs, event logs, and disk overlay snapshots allows active trajectories to migrate across physical worker nodes without task loss.

Section 10.7 (Log Compaction Policies): Trajectory storage must enforce multi-tier lifecycle compaction, pruning bulky ephemeral observation bytes while preserving the causal decision graph across Hot, Warm, and Cold storage tiers.

Section 10.8 (Trajectory Storage Engines): Production trajectory persistence requires a hybrid engine pairing embedded LSM-trees or relational WALs for synchronous per-turn logging with columnar object storage for archival analytics.
